items.title: 10.1 Force on a current-carrying conductor in a uniform magnetic field

source_refs.note: Topic 10.1 as printed (PDF 230-232, printed 227-229): Figs. 10.2 to 10.4, the Do You Know? and Interesting Information boxes, Eqs. 10.1 to 10.3 and Example 10.1. Fig. 10.2 carries a Book correction.

blocks.text: It has been observed experimentally that a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force. Consider a straight conductor carrying a steady current placed perpendicular to uniform magnetic field. Assume the direction of the current is out of the paper as shown by ⊙ in Fig. 10.2. The direction of magnetic field produced by the current is also shown.

Just as two magnets exert forces on each other through their magnetic fields, a current-carrying conductor experiences a force due to the interaction between its own magnetic field and the external magnetic field. To determine the direction of this force, consider the interaction between the two fields.

blocks.alt: A conductor seen end-on, with a dot showing the current out of the paper, sits between two pole blocks: S above and N below. Vertical field lines run upward from N to S. Blue circles with anticlockwise arrows show the conductor's own field. A force arrow F points horizontally to the left.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.2: A current-carrying conductor in a uniform magnetic field: current out of the paper and force F (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.2).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 10.2 puts N above S, which makes the field point downward; with the current out of the paper the force F = I L x B would then point to the right. To match the text's force to the left, the poles are drawn with S above and N below (field upward).

The magnetic field produced by the current and the external uniform magnetic field reinforce each other on the right side of the conductor and cancel each other on the left side. Consequently, the conductor moves towards the side where the field is weaker. That is, the force on the conductor is directed to the left. Thus, the force F is perpendicular to both the conductor and the magnetic field. Fleming's left-hand rule is used to predict the direction of the force experienced by a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. To apply the rule:

blocks.title: Fleming's left-hand rule
blocks.text: Position your left hand such that the first finger points in the direction of magnetic field, the second finger points in the direction of current, the thumb will then point in the direction of force.
However direction of force can also be found by using right hand rule that can be stated as:

blocks.title: Right hand rule
blocks.text: Curl fingers of your right hand from current to magnetic field through small angle, the stretched thumb will indicate the direction of force.
The Fleming's left hand rule is illustrated in Fig. 10.3.

blocks.alt: A left hand with the thumb pointing straight up, labelled Force; the first finger pointing to the upper right, labelled Magnetic Field; and the second finger pointing to the lower right, labelled Current. The three are at right angles to one another; the other two fingers are folded.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.3: Fleming's left-hand rule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.3).

blocks.alt: A bar magnet, S half green on the left and N half red on the right, with curved field lines leaving the N end and returning to the S end; arrows on the lines point away from N and towards S, and the lines do not cross.
blocks.caption: Do You Know? (PDF page 230): Magnetic field lines of a bar magnet (original drawing after the textbook's picture in this box).

blocks.text: Let us now determine the magnitude of the force on a current-carrying conductor placed inside a magnetic field. Experimentally, it has been observed that the magnitude of the force acting on the conductor is directly proportional to the current I in the conductor, the length L of the conductor, and the strength of the external magnetic field B. The strength of the magnetic field is also known as the magnetic induction B, which has the same direction as the field. From Eq. (10.1) we can see that B = F/IL, so we can define B as:

blocks.title: Magnetic field strength
blocks.text: The magnetic strength is numerically equal to the force exerted on a conductor of length one metre carrying one ampere current, placed perpendicular to the magnetic field.
Equation B = F/IL also gives us the unit of B. The SI unit of B is tesla (T).
It may be noted that magnetic induction is a vector quantity. Its direction is that of magnetic field.
We can also consider a vector L which has a magnitude equal to the length of the conductor and its direction is along the flow of current.

blocks.title: Interesting Information
blocks.text: The Earth's magnetic field is approximately that of a dipole, like that of the fictitious bar magnet. Where the south magnetic pole is towards the geographic north pole and the north magnetic pole is towards the geographic south pole.

blocks.alt: The Earth with a fictitious bar magnet inside, tilted slightly from the geographic axis (dashed). Field lines loop round the Earth from its southern half to its northern half like those of a dipole. Labels: South magnetic pole and Geographic North pole at the top; Geographic South pole and North magnetic pole at the bottom.

blocks.title: Example 10.1
blocks.problem: A 20.0 cm wire carrying a current of 10.0 A is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.30 T. If the wire makes an angle of 40° with the direction of magnetic field, find the magnitude of the force acting on the wire.
steps: Length of the wire = L = 20.0 cm = 0.20 m
Strength of magnetic field = B = 0.30 T
Substituting the values in Eq. (10.2): F = 10.0 A × 0.30 T × 0.20 m × sin 40° = 0.39 N
